lines.note: The headword points back to `Faqidaxi`, hakidashi, “sweeping out.” The extra printed `i` is retained rather than silently regularized; `Vide` means “see.”
`Faqimono` is ハキモノ, footwear. The gloss starts with shoes and sandals, not the sweeping sense of the neighboring `faqi` compounds.
“Of Japan, etc.” completes the footwear examples on the preceding line; this fragment is Portuguese, not a new entry.
ハキノゴイ combines sweeping and wiping clean. Portuguese `Varrendo alimpar` means cleaning by sweeping; the listed endings belong to the conjugation of nogou.

`Vare cagami` is ワレ カガミ, a broken mirror, supporting the Sino-Japanese compound 破鏡. The long-vowel mark in the headword is preserved as transcribed rather than changed solely from the expected lexical reading.
ハキソエ means wearing an additional sword: `cingir` here is girding on a weapon. This is another meaning of haku, distinct from sweeping or putting on footwear.
The additional weapon is described as a long sword or a montante; this completes the definition of `Faqiſoye`.
ハキステ is sweeping away/discarding. The Portuguese explicitly combines sweeping with throwing out, confirming the compound's second element sute.
ハキタメ means gathering by sweeping. The listed -muru form appears in the following example, introduced by `Vt`.
チリヲ ハキタムル is gathering dust or rubbish by sweeping. Portuguese `cisco` identifies the small refuse being collected; the nasal abbreviations are retained.
ハキタテ is raising something through sweeping. The gloss continues with `co-` plus `mo`, “such as,” not a Japanese fragment.
Together with the preceding fragment this reads “such as dust, etc.” Historical `poo` is the dust stirred up by sweeping.

runs.text: O cingir mais hũ montante menor,

lines.note: ハキゾエ is the noun for wearing an additional, smaller sword. The printed voiced `z` is retained despite the unvoiced spelling in the related verbal entry above.
“Or shorter” further specifies the additional sword; it is a continuation of the preceding noun definition.
ハラ here is 原, an open plain or field. The next headword has the same sound but a different sense.
ハラ here is 腹, the belly. ハラヲ タツル introduces the idiom for becoming angry; the Portuguese word continues as `Agas-taſe` on the next line.
ハラガ タツ is the parallel intransitive anger idiom. `Idem` assigns the same meaning; final `Fa-` starts the following example's `Farauo` across the line break.

runs.text: rauo qiri, l, caqiqiru, l, ſuru.

lines.note: With preceding `Fa-`, this is ハラヲ キリ, with alternative verbs kakikiru and suru. The Portuguese begins the explanation of cutting one's belly; isolated `l` is Latin “or,” not Japanese.
The first gloss ends “the belly, or kill oneself.” A new honorific example begins ハラヲ メサ-, continued by the next row; do not read the fragment as a complete verb.

runs.text: Cortar a barriga peſſoa nobre, ou ma-

lines.note: The sense is a noble person's cutting their belly, followed by “or killing oneself.” Japanese `meſa-iuru` is suspicious: the expected honorific is mesaruru. The first letter of this damaged continuation needs particular care; the transcription is not normalized from grammar alone.
The noble person acts “with their own hands.” Final ハラガ begins the next idiom and belongs with `iru` below, not with this Portuguese clause.
ハラガ イル and ハラヲ スユル express anger subsiding or being settled. `Aplacarſe a ira` confirms the emotional, rather than anatomical, sense.

This is the idiom 腹が下る, having diarrhea; `camaras` here concerns bowel movements, not rooms. Printed `cudau` is suspicious beside expected cudaru, but the weak internal area is not securely resolved by the meaning alone.
ハラガ トマル is the converse: the diarrhea stops. The Portuguese infinitive describes the stopping of the bowel discharges.
ハラアテ and ハラマキ name armor protecting the torso. Portuguese `Armas` has the broader equipment/armor sense here, not merely an offensive weapon.
ハラカ names a fish. The gloss only says “a certain fish,” so a modern species identification would exceed the evidence on this line.
ハラカラ is explained by キョゥダイ, siblings. The synonym is visibly upright Japanese, not italic Portuguese; the gloss specifies brother or sister.
ハラクダリ is the noun for diarrhea, matching the earlier abdominal idiom. This reinforces the bodily meaning of Portuguese `Camaras` in this cluster.
ハラダチ is anger or irritation, a noun. Portuguese `Agaſtamento` contrasts with the reflexive verb in the next entry.
This is the conjugating verb haradatsu, to become angry, with the past form haradatta. The `u` ending is joined to the verb stem, not an independent word.

runs.text: Adu. Modo de chouer, ou corre-

lines.note: ハラハラト describes falling rain or flowing tears. The scan reads `corre-`, completed as correrem below; OCR `torre-` did not produce the verb required by the clause.

runs.text: rem as lagrimas, ou de derrubar, & cortar

lines.note: “Tears flowing, or felling and cutting…” continues the adverb's uses. The military example that follows extends the image to enemies falling in succession.

The enlarged scan has a descending p and a broken tall l in `polos`, not the first-pass conjecture todos. The phrase describes cutting through the enemies; historical polos corresponds to pelos. テキヲ ハラ- starts the Japanese example, continued below.

Together the Japanese is テキヲ ハラハラト キリフセテ, cutting enemies down. The t in the continuation of farafarato is weakly printed; its established transcription remains a contextual reading, not a new spelling.
This completes `der-rubando`, “felling enemies,” and closes the military example of farafarato.

runs.text: Cinta, ou corda com que cingem,

lines.note: ハラガケ is a belly strap or rope. The following line identifies the animal and explains its restraining purpose, distinguishing it from the armor entries.

runs.text: & amarrão ao cauallo pora que ſe não deite.

lines.note: The strap is fastened around a horse so that it will not lie down. The unusual-looking `pora` is retained from the scan rather than modernized to para.
ハラガワリ is expanded to ハラガワリノコ, children of different mothers. The explanatory `i` introduces a Japanese synonym, not part of its reading.
The first clause supplies “different mothers.” ハラガワリノ キョゥダイ then makes the sibling relationship explicit; the spelling retains the source's long-vowel mark.
“Siblings, children of different mothers” translates the preceding Japanese phrase. It identifies maternal difference without requiring a modernized spelling of mãys.

runs.text: Criança que fica no ventre da

lines.note: ハラゴメ names a child still in the womb. The definition is qualified by the father's death on the following line, not simply pregnancy in general.
The child remains unborn when the father dies. Upright `X` is a label; `Farago-` begins the following Japanese example across the physical break.
ハラゴメノ トキカラ テテガ シンダ means the father died while the child was still unborn. The scan supports `tetega`, with tete “father,” rather than OCR `terega`; the Portuguese repeats the father's death.

runs.text: olhe o pay ficando, ou eſtando ainda no ven-

lines.note: Joined to `Morre-`, this describes the father dying while the child is still in the womb. The attached pronoun `lhe` refers to the child; `ven-` continues ventre below.

runs.text: tre da mãy. ¶ Item, Criança, ou filho de qual

lines.note: The maternal womb completes the first sense. `Item` introduces a related sense involving offspring of an animal, continued below.

runs.text: quer animal que fica no ventre da mãy morta.

lines.note: This second sense concerns offspring remaining in a dead mother's womb. It differs from the first sense, where the father has died.

ハラゴモリ is a small unborn deer in its mother's belly. The scan reads `Faragomori`, also supported by the NINJAL headword index; the OCR's extra i produced an implausible -myori sequence. The gloss continues in column 2.

runs.text: da cerua que matarão, o qual ſe come.

lines.note: The unborn deer is taken from a killed doe and is eaten. This closes `Faragomori` from the bottom of column 1; it is not a new headword.
ハライ is harau, shaking off or expelling. The long-vowel endings describe the historical conjugation, and the examples extend from dust to metaphorical senses.
チリ ホコリヲ ハロゥ is shaking off dust. Final `A-` belongs to the following `Atariuo`, which begins a different idiom.
アタリヲ ハロゥ is proceeding with imposing pomp, as the Portuguese `grande fauſto` explains. The next `A-` starts `Acuuo` across the break.
アクヲ ハロゥ means casting out evil; the Portuguese interprets it as ridding oneself of sins. `Te-` starts the following example, not the current word.
テマエヲ ハロゥ is explained as clearing or justifying oneself concerning something. The gloss continues with settlement of accounts, another extension of harau.

ハライ カタノ サンヨゥ refers to an account of expenditure. The scan supports long s and a circumflex in `ſanyô`; 算用 and the following Portuguese accounting gloss independently explain why OCR `fanyǒ` is suspect.

runs.text: Contas do que hum tem deſpendido, por or-

lines.note: These are accounts of what someone has spent, with `or-` beginning ordem. The subject is expenditure recorded on another's authority, not the expulsion sense above.
“By order or commission of the lord” completes the accounting definition. `commiſão` denotes an entrusted commission, not a fee in the modern financial sense.

runs.text: O cortar tudo ſem ter deuer que ſe

lines.note: ハライギリ is indiscriminate cutting down. The gloss says without regard to whom the victim may be; `ſe` is the first part of seja, whose `ja` is on the next physical line.
This completes preceding `ſe` as seja: woman, child, religious person, etc. The scan has only `ja` at the start, so the OCR's repeated `ſe` was removed. `Farai-` starts the Japanese example below.
With the preceding fragment, ハライギリヲ スル means performing that indiscriminate cutting. This short row is Japanese body text, not a catchword.
ハライノケ is casting something off or aside. The Portuguese offers synonymous verbs, the second split as lan-çar over two rows.
“Throw outside/away” completes lançar fora from the preceding row and finishes the definition of harainokeru.
ハライステ is assigned the same discarding sense. The explicitly written `tçuru` ending is retained; it is not replaced by the more abbreviated uru convention elsewhere.
ハラマキ names armor, as it did as an alternative to faraate in column 1. The short Portuguese gloss should be read with that martial context.
ハラメカシ describes causing a clattering or rattling sound. The Portuguese begins with making a noisy commotion; the next line specifies contact with armor.

runs.text: ruido no cortar dando pollas armas, &c.

lines.note: The noise is produced in cutting or striking against armor. `pollas armas` supplies the material setting for the preceding sound-producing verb.
ハラメキ is the corresponding occurrence of rattling or clattering, rather than actively causing it. Its -qu ending yields harameku.

runs.text: ruido. ¶ Item, Eſtarem algũas couſas mal

lines.note: After completing the noise sense, `Item` introduces a different application: things being poorly cooked. The following examples are grains, so the shift is substantive.

runs.text: cozidas, & deſunidas como grãos de arroz,

lines.note: The poorly cooked things remain separate, exemplified by rice grains. The gloss concerns a loose, insufficiently cohesive texture rather than sound in this second sense.
The second food example reads `gergelada`, with a visible ascender on d, not OCR c. メシガ ハラメク then applies the texture description to cooked rice.

runs.text: Eſtar o arroz mal cozido deſta maneira.

lines.note: “The rice being poorly cooked in this manner” explicitly translates the preceding example and confirms that mexi is the food rather than an unrelated verb.
ハラミ is conceiving or being pregnant. コヲ begins the transitive-looking expression “carry a child,” completed by faramu below; the long-vowel past ending is retained from the print.

runs.text: Eſtar prenhe, ou com o filho na bar-

lines.note: コヲ ハラム is being with child. Portuguese `prenhe` and “with the child in the belly” explain the state, with barriga divided over the row boundary.
ムギ, or イネガ ハラム, extends the swelling/pregnancy image to grain crops. The isolated `l` offers an alternative crop name rather than a Japanese syllable.

runs.text: o trigo, ou arroz pera eſpigar.

lines.note: The wheat or rice is about to come into ear. This explains the agricultural sense of haramu, not literal animal pregnancy.
ハラン, 波瀾, is equated with ナミ, waves. The Portuguese `Ondas` confirms the concrete wave sense rather than only the modern metaphor of turmoil.

runs.text: Hũa maneira de grãos como bagos

lines.note: ハララゴ is described as little grains like berries. The following comparison with shiny red grapes is consistent with roe, but the gloss itself describes appearance rather than naming a fish species.
“Of red and shiny grapes” completes the visual comparison for hararago. Historical `vuas` is the grape word, not a Japanese example.
ハラリハラリト is another repeated adverb describing flowing or falling. The Portuguese verb correrem leads into tears on the next row.

runs.text: lagrimas, ou de chouer. ¶ Itẽ, Modo de eſ-

lines.note: The first sense concerns tears or rain. `Itẽ` starts a second sense involving the condition of rice, linking this adverb with the texture vocabulary above.

runs.text: tar o arroz duro, & mal cozido. Vt,

lines.note: The rice is hard and undercooked. `Mexi-` begins the Japanese example and joins the next row's ga; the physical division is preserved rather than rewriting the sentence on one line.
メシガ ハラリハラリト スル predicates this loose, hard texture of rice. The example completes the preceding definition without introducing a new entry.
ハラリト is here given the totalizing meaning “entirely, completely.” This particular gloss must not be replaced by the better-known modern falling-motion sense.
ハラワタ is the intestines or entrails. Portuguese `Tripas` is a direct anatomical equivalent.

runs.text: Hũa cinta que poem as molheres

lines.note: ハラヲビ is an abdominal sash. The Portuguese identifies the wearers as women, with pregnancy and purpose specified in the continuation.

runs.text: prenhes junto da carne pera fazer a barriga pe-

lines.note: Pregnant women wear the sash next to the skin to keep the belly small. This records the dictionary's description of a practice, not an endorsement or modern health recommendation.
This completes `pe-quena`, “small.” The upright X is a label, not Japanese body text requiring a kana reading.
ハラシ means clearing or dispelling. The scan supports `Cocoro`, heart/mind, rather than OCR `Cocoru`; it joins the object marker on the next line.
ココロヲ ハラス is relieving one's feelings; Portuguese `Deſabafar` has f, not the OCR's long s, consistent with the visible letter and verb. フシヲ ハラ- begins the next expression for resolving a doubt.
フシヲ ハラス is resolving a doubt, as `Soltar a duuida` states. マヨイヲ ハラ- begins another dispelling expression, now concerning error or delusion.
マヨイヲ ハラス casts out error. キヅカイヲ then introduces cares or worries; the printed zz is retained in the reading aid's historical distinction.

runs.text: Botar de ſi os cuidados, ou tristeza.

lines.note: キヅカイヲ ハラス is ridding oneself of worries or sadness. The Portuguese names both cuidados and tristeza, broadening the emotional range of the expression.
ノゾミヲ ハラス means fulfilling wishes. This is satisfaction of desire, not its rejection; the Portuguese explicitly says to fulfil the desires.
ハラヤ names a kind of cushion or bolster according to `aluaçade`. The brief gloss does not establish a more specific modern object identification.

runs.text: Couſa publica, ou onde ha concurſo de

lines.note: ハレ is the public or conspicuous sphere, rather than clear weather in this entry. The gloss describes something public or a place with an assembly of people.
“People” completes the public-gathering definition above. The separate `Fare` at the right is the catchword, not part of this body sentence.
